maths.problem: A mango is in the left bag and a lemon is in the right bag. The left side is down. Meena swaps the two things. Which side goes down now?
maths.explain: The left side was down, so the mango is heavier. The mango is heavier wherever it sits. After the swap the mango is on the right. So the right side goes down.
maths.context: In the Hand and Hanger Test, the bag with the heavier thing went down. This asks what happens when the two things change places.
maths.why_maths: Knowing which thing is heavier lets you say what the balance will do before you look.

maths.problem: On the hanger, the coconut beat the mango. Then the mango beat the lemon. Kavya has not tested the coconut against the lemon. Which will go down?
maths.explain: The coconut is heavier than the mango. The mango is heavier than the lemon. So the coconut is heavier than the lemon too. Kavya can know this without testing.
maths.context: In the Hand and Hanger Test you compared two things at a time. This puts two results together.
maths.why_maths: Putting two results together saves a test. You can order three things with only two looks at the balance.

maths.problem: All the potatoes are alike. The left bag has 5 potatoes. The right bag has 3. How many potatoes must Devi add to the right bag to make the two bags level?
maths.explain: The potatoes are alike, so the same number means the same weight. Count on from 3 to 5: 4, 5. That is 2 more. Then both bags have 5.
maths.context: In Two Bags to Carry, you made two bags of vegetables level. This asks how many more are needed when all the things are alike.
maths.why_maths: When things are alike, you can count instead of weighing. Finding the gap tells you how many to add.

maths.problem: A ball of dough is level with 6 coins. Lakshmi rolls the ball into a long snake. Then she cuts the snake into 2 equal pieces. How many coins is one piece level with?
maths.explain: Rolling does not change the weight, so the snake is still level with 6 coins. The 2 equal pieces share that weight. 6 is 3 and 3. So one piece is level with 3 coins.
maths.context: In Squash the Dough, a new shape did not change the weight. This adds one cut into two equal pieces.
maths.why_maths: If the shape does not change the weight, you only have to think about the cut. Half the dough is half the weight.

maths.problem: On Earth, a potato is level with an onion. On the Moon every thing weighs less. An astronaut takes the balance, the potato and the onion to the Moon. What does the balance do there?
maths.explain: On the Moon the potato weighs less. The onion weighs less too, by just as much. Both sides get lighter together, so neither side goes down. A balance only compares the two sides.
maths.context: In the Hand and Hanger Test, the hanger stayed level when two things weighed the same. This takes a level balance to the Moon.
maths.why_maths: A balance compares. If both sides change in the same way, the answer does not change.

roots.context: We lifted things and tested them on a balance. Now we ask what 'heavy' really is, and where the feeling of heavy comes from.

deep_truth.truth: In the Two Boxes Surprise, the small box and the big box hung level on the hanger. In your hands, the small box felt heavier. The boxes had not changed. So how heavy a thing feels comes from the thing and from you together. A balance compares only the two things.
deep_truth.habit: We think our hands simply read how heavy a thing is, the way eyes read a number on a page. But the feeling of heavy is made partly by us: by our eyes, our arms and what we expect. That is why people everywhere made balances.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Two Boxes Surprise, two boxes that were level on the hanger felt different in your hands. In the Hand and Hanger Test, your hands could not be sure about the potato and the onion, and the hanger could.

three.who_am_i: When you lift a box, your eyes, your arms and your guesses all work together. What you feel is partly the box and partly you.
three.what_is_life: A squirrel flicks her head to feel a nut. A crow watches things swing in the wind. Many living beings judge weight, each in their own way.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth pulls on every thing, all the time: the lemon, the coconut, the hanger and you. Weight is that pull.

roots.thread: There is one Earth, and it pulls on every thing. That one pull shows up as many weights: small for a groundnut, large for a coconut. When a balance is level, the Earth is pulling the two sides by the same amount, even if they look nothing alike. And when the bags are empty, the hanger is level too. Nothing on one side balances nothing on the other.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha tells of a king who asked people born blind to touch an elephant. One touched the ear, one the leg, one the tail. Each said the elephant was like the part they had touched, and they quarrelled.
teachings.link: Your eyes said the big box was heavier. Your hands said the small box was heavier. The hanger said they were the same. Each one met the boxes in a different way.

teachings.teaching: Socrates asks: when the same wind blows, does it not feel cold to one of us and not to the other? He is explaining the idea of a thinker named Protagoras, that the wind is cold for the one who feels cold.
teachings.link: A bucket of water is heavy for you and light for a grown-up. The small box felt heavy to your hand. The feeling depends on who is lifting.

teachings.teaching: These verses say that the sky was raised and the balance was set. They ask people to weigh fairly and not to give less than the balance shows.
teachings.link: People long ago saw that a seller's hand could not be trusted to judge weight, even an honest hand. So they agreed to trust the balance.

science.text: When a small thing and a big thing weigh the same, the small one feels heavier to most people. Augustin Charpentier showed this in 1891. It has been tested many times since, with children as well as grown-ups.

Why does it happen? Many scientists think the eyes expect the big thing to be heavier, and the surprise changes the feeling. Others have found that this cannot be the whole reason. Nobody is sure yet.

other_view.who: Many scientists who study weight and forces
other_view.view: They say the weight of a box is a plain fact about the box and the Earth. It is the same whoever lifts it, and even when nobody lifts it. The small box only seemed heavier. That was a mistake made by the body, and the balance put it right.

practice.title: Heavy arms
practice.say: Stand up. Hold both arms straight out to the sides. Close your eyes. I will count slowly to thirty. Feel your arms as I count. Now let them down slowly. Did your arms get heavier while I counted? Did they really change? Where did the feeling of heavy come from?
practice.kid: Hold your arms straight out. Close your eyes. Count slowly to thirty. Do your arms feel heavier? Did they really get heavier?

ask: The small box felt heavier, and the balance said they were the same. Which one was right? Could both be right in some way?
Is a bucket of water heavy if nobody ever tries to lift it?
A squirrel and you both lift the same groundnut. Does it feel the same to both of you?
Why do you think people everywhere chose to trust a balance more than a hand?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that hands cannot be trusted to judge weight? This card tells the true story, from the first balances to a test with two balls.
how_we_found_out.story: For a very long time, people judged weight by lifting. A handful of grain was traded for a handful of salt. But hands do not agree with each other, and people quarrelled. So people made balances. More than 4,000 years ago, traders in the Indus cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro used balances with small cubes of stone as weights. The cubes found at one city match those found at another, far away. Still, many people believed that a careful hand feels weight just as it is. In 1834 a German scientist, Ernst Weber, tested this. He asked people to lift two weights and say which was heavier. When the weights were close, people could not tell. Then in 1891 a French doctor, Augustin Charpentier, gave people two balls of the same weight, one small and one large. Almost everyone said the small ball was heavier. The hand does not simply read weight. It can be fooled by size.
how_we_found_out.who: Traders of the Indus cities, Ernst Weber and Augustin Charpentier
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A careful hand feels the weight of a thing just as it is. Weber's test in 1834 showed that hands cannot tell close weights apart. Charpentier's test in 1891 showed that a small ball feels heavier than a large ball of the same weight.

playtest: Walked through every flow on paper as a parent and a six-year-old in a flat. Nothing was built or lifted for this check, so try each part once yourself. The hanger balance needs care: the hanger must swing freely, the two bags must be the same kind, and the empty balance must be level. In the Hand and Hanger Test the spoon, the potato and the lemon should win their pairs clearly. The potato and onion pair has no fixed answer, on purpose. For the Two Boxes Surprise, keep each box light enough for one small hand. Most people feel the small box as heavier, but a few do not, and younger children feel it less strongly than older ones. If your child feels no difference, their hands agreed with the hanger, and that is a fine result too. A plastic hanger can bend under two full bags of vegetables, so Two Bags to Carry uses small vegetables and says what to do if it bends. In the Odd Packet, the packets hold 2, 2 and 3 coins. One coin should tip a light hanger. If it does not, use 4, 4 and 6. Heavier Takes It was checked on paper: the 12 things are far enough apart in weight that the order is not in doubt. Step minutes add up to each part's minutes.
